newsitem.title: USA: Sen. D'Amato promises action on mortgage insurance.
newsitem.headline: Sen. D'Amato promises action on mortgage insurance.

text.p: Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato vowed on Wednesday to move forward legislation to curtail unneccessary mortgage insurance.
The bill, which passed the House of Representatives in April on a 421 to seven vote, has been held up by some Republicans voicing objections from the insurance industry.
D'Amato had been seeking a compromise approach that would be acceptable to all parties, but at a hearing on lending disclosure laws, the New York Republican said his patience was wearing thin.
"To my colleagues, I say to you, Alfonse has not stopped," D'Amato said. "I will at an appropriate time bring an amendment on the floor."
D'Amato said he would seek to attach the private mortgage insurance restrictions to unrelated, popular legislation in order to force a vote.
The legislation passed by the House, H.R. 607 known as the Homeowners Insurance Protection Act, would allow homeowners to cancel mortgage insurance when they build up sufficient equity.

Currently, mortgage lenders require a borrower to obtain and pay for such insurance when the borrower is making a relatively small down payment, such as five percent of the purchase price of a home. Borrowers putting down 20 percent or more generally are not required to obtain insurance, which can cost $300 to $900 a year.

The House bill would automatically cancel a mortgage insurance policy if the homeowner was current on mortgage payments and had built up 25 percent equity of the original value of the house. Homeowner's equity is the value of the home after subtracting the remaining principal on a mortgage.
Consumer advocates, who strongly backed the bill, feared that the measure might die in the Senate after D'Amato's committee postponed in April a planned vote on the bill.
D'Amato said Wednesday he would move the legislation one way or another. "We can do it the nice way or we can do it a way some of my colleagues will not enjoy," he said.
If Republicans opposed to the bill to not agree to a compromise, D'Amato said he would introduce a bill containing the same provisions as the measure passed by the House.
